traits.leaf_incision.note: DELTA, Rosaceae (read 2026-10-17): simple blades either undivided or dissected. Wikipedia (read 2026-10-17): Prunus leaves unlobed, Cotoneaster entire, Crataegus with lobed or serrated margins, Rubus simple, lobed or compound, Sorbus (Torminalis) maple-like lobes. Weighted by the large unlobed genera (Prunus, Cotoneaster, most Crataegus) and by compound-leaved Rubus/Rosa/Potentilla, whose leaflets are not cut.

traits.leaf_margin.note: Flora of China family account (read 2026-10-17): blade margin often saw-toothed, only rarely smooth. DELTA (read 2026-10-17) lists crenate, serrate and dentate margins with entire ones fairly infrequent; Wikipedia Rosaceae says the margin is most often serrate and the Rose page gives serrated leaflets. Cotoneaster (entire) is the main exception among big genera.

traits.stamens.note: Simpson, Plant Systematics (2019) p. 325, 327: stamens 20 to many, rarely 1 or 5, arising centripetally. Book writes ∞ (numerous); 200 is our stand-in for the upper bound and 20 for 'numerous' with no stated lower bound.

traits.carpels.note: Simpson, Plant Systematics (2019) p. 325, 327: carpels 1 to many, gynoecium apocarpous or syncarpous (one in Prunus, five in the apple group, many in Rosa and Fragaria). Book writes ∞; 50 is our stand-in for the upper bound.

traits.corolla_shape.note: Simpson, Plant Systematics (2019) p. 325: corolla apopetalous, usually 5 free petals on the hypanthium rim. Free petals: rotate by PlantGen's free-petal rule; the book names no other corolla form.

traits.note: Jepson's Manual of the Flowering Plants of California (1925), read in full: flowers regular, commonly perfect; calyx 5 (or 4)-lobed; petals 5, rarely none; stamens 10 to numerous, inserted with the petals on the calyx or on a disk lining the calyx-tube (a hypanthium); pistils 1 to many, free from the calyx, or united in an ovary nearly or wholly inferior, as in the pomes (Amelanchier, Malus); in the other tribes the ovary is superior.

traits.leaf_arrangement.note: Hutchinson (vol. 1, 2nd ed., 1959), family 24 Rosaceae: trees, shrubs or herbs; leaves of many kinds, simple or compound, alternate or rarely opposite; stipules mostly present, in pairs, sometimes joined to the leaf stalk.

traits.leaf_division.note: Hutchinson (vol. 1, 2nd ed., 1959), family 24 Rosaceae: trees, shrubs or herbs; leaves of many kinds, simple or compound, alternate or rarely opposite; stipules mostly present, in pairs, sometimes joined to the leaf stalk.

traits.leaf_habit.note: Watson and Dallwitz, The Families of Flowering Plants (DELTA data, items edited May 2026), family Rosaceae as that work draws it, there coded together with Guamatelaceae, Quillajaceae, Stylobasiaceae: how long the leaves last (character 37), coded usually deciduous, sometimes evergreen. Read from the coded states by script (spec-rework/b1/delta/mapdelta.py with character 21 added); states the authors do not qualify, side by side, read as often.

traits.rosette.note: APweb, Rosales page, Rosaceae (read 2026-10-16): of about 2,805 species, Amygdaloideae (about 1,540) are woody and Rosoideae run from herbs to shrubs; DELTA Rosaceae says only some herbs have a basal cluster of leaves; so no rosette is usual and a basal one sometimes.

traits.life_span.note: Watson and Dallwitz, The Families of Flowering Plants (DELTA data, items edited May 2026), family Rosaceae as that work draws it, there coded together with Guamatelaceae, Quillajaceae, Stylobasiaceae: the herbs' life form (character 21), coded perennial. Read from the coded states by script (spec-rework/b1/delta/mapdelta.py with character 21 added); states the authors do not qualify, side by side, read as often.

traits.phyllotaxis_pattern.note: Simpson, Plant Systematics (2019) p. 325, 327, 328, family Rosaceae: phyllotaxis pattern spiral (rarely opposite), usually; read as {"spiral": "usually"}.

traits.stipules.note: Simpson, Plant Systematics (2019) p. 325, 327, 328, family Rosaceae: stipules true, often fused to petiole base, usually; read as {"true": "usually"}.

traits.fruit_type.note: Wikipedia Rosaceae and Rubus (read 2026-10-17): genus sizes there put the aggregates first: Rubus (250 to over 1,000 spp, drupelet aggregate) with Potentilla (~500, a head of achenes), Fragaria and Geum, against pomes of Sorbus, Crataegus and Cotoneaster (~260 each, ~800-900 with Malus, Pyrus) and Prunus drupes (~340). Single achenes (Alchemilla ~270, Rosa hips ~100) added as sometimes. Margin depends on Rubus's count. Re-ranks the earlier value, from diversity-evolution-land-plants, whose top states were tied.

traits.ovary_position.note: Added kinds only; the usual kind's source is the family's `traits` note. The books add half_inferior (sometimes): Ingrouille, Diversity and Evolution of Land Plants (1992) p. 161, 163, 164: superior, half_inferior or inferior.
